The mismatched lot description may reveal a more fundamental problem with the proposed conveyance. Prioritize the effect on the agreed transaction rather than the mere length of the report. The report's date also matters. New judgments, liens, conveyances, or other events can arise before recording. Closing procedures and the issued policy address the relevant time and insured conditions. A report obtained months earlier is not an assurance that nothing has changed. The agent should follow the title provider's current requirements and communicate new information affecting the transaction.

454.title: Owner and lender policies protect different interests
454.text: Owner and lender policies protect separate interests; endorsements and expanded coverage depend on actual terms rather than guaranteeing the buyer's intended use. An owner's policy protects the insured ownership interest against covered title losses. A lender's policy protects the lender's security interest and priority. The buyer should not assume that paying for the lender's policy insures the buyer's equity. The prior owner's policy also does not automatically insure a new purchaser. Title insurance generally addresses covered defects connected to the insured title, often arising before the policy date, rather than functioning like a promise that the property will never experience a future problem. Coverage depends on the named insured, estate, amount, covered risks, exclusions, exceptions, and conditions. Standard and extended coverage differ. Exam descriptions often associate standard coverage with specified record and hidden title risks and extended coverage with additional matters that may require a survey or inspection. Neither is unlimited. Do not conclude that every unrecorded interest is excluded from every standard policy or that extended coverage guarantees building condition, zoning compliance, and all future uses. The title premium is commonly paid once for the issued policy. Who pays is generally negotiated subject to applicable rules, not fixed by one statewide custom. The party's choice of insurer and federal restrictions in covered transactions should be respected. A seller cannot simply dictate a buyer-paid title provider in violation of applicable RESPA rules.

455.title: Insurance does not replace the purchase bargain
455.text: A buyer requires legal access suitable for commercial deliveries. A proposed title policy excepts the recorded access easement, and the easement document appears to permit only limited residential use. The fact that a title insurer will issue a policy does not mean the access meets the buyer's operating needs. A policy can insure title subject to a restriction that makes the buyer's planned use impractical. Similarly, a lender may accept a policy satisfying its security requirements while the buyer wants additional protection or investigation. The lender and buyer have different interests. Loan approval does not establish that every title condition acceptable to the lender is acceptable to the buyer. An endorsement can modify coverage for a stated risk, subject to underwriting and its terms. The agent should not promise that a requested endorsement is available or eliminates the underlying condition. Insurance can allocate certain losses; it does not necessarily remove an easement, relocate a boundary, or legalize a nonpermitted structure. Resolve the client's substantive concern and the insurance question separately.

456.title: Escrow is conditional custody
456.text: Escrow holds conditional deliveries and follows authorized instructions; possession of all funds and a signed deed does not waive an unresolved condition. Escrow holds money, documents, or other items until specified conditions are satisfied, then delivers them according to instructions. It permits the buyer and seller to exchange performance through a neutral holder. The buyer need not hand over the full price without the agreed title transfer, and the seller need not release an effective deed without the required payment conditions. The escrow holder is a limited agent with duties defined by the instructions and law. It should act impartially within that role, safeguard funds, and follow consistent authorized instructions. It does not become the buyer's negotiator, the seller's legal adviser, or an arbiter empowered to settle disputed contract rights. Written instructions identify the conditions for closing, documents to record, liens to pay, expenses to allocate, and parties to receive funds. Supplemental or amended instructions must be authorized appropriately. One party's telephone request does not ordinarily authorize a change that affects the other party's rights.

457.title: Conditions control disbursement
457.text: Suppose the buyer deposits all required funds and the seller deposits a signed deed, but a required lien release remains unavailable. Physical possession of money and documents does not necessarily authorize closing. Escrow must satisfy the applicable instructions and requirements before releasing the conditional deliveries. If the parties agree to close despite a changed condition, proper amended instructions and any required lender or insurer approvals must be obtained. One party cannot ordinarily direct escrow to ignore a condition benefiting the other. Nor can the agent privately assure escrow that the principals "will be fine with it" without the needed authority and documentation. The same principle applies to early release of a deposit. Money held pending conditions is not unrestricted seller money just because the seller requests it for moving expenses. Releasing it can change the buyer's position and requires the applicable authorization. A later dispute is harder to resolve if funds have already been disbursed improperly; the escrow holder's neutral role is intended to prevent that unilateral shift.

458.title: Who regulates the escrow holder
458.text: Independent escrow licensing and specified professional exemptions follow different rules; a brokerage exemption is not unlimited permission to operate public escrow services. Independent escrow companies are licensed under California's Escrow Law by the Department of Financial Protection and Innovation. Other lawful escrow providers operate under specified exemptions and supervision associated with their profession or business, including qualifying title operations, banks, attorneys, and real estate brokers. A real estate broker's exemption is limited to qualifying transactions in which the broker acts as an agent or party and performs licensed activity. It is not permission to operate an unrelated independent escrow business for the public without meeting the applicable requirements. A salesperson does not independently acquire a separate escrow-business license by holding a real estate license. The important exam distinction is between an independent DFPI-licensed escrow and an escrow lawfully handled under a specific exemption. "Exempt from this licensing requirement" does not mean exempt from all fiduciary obligations, trust rules, or professional supervision.

459.title: Follow the closing sequence
459.text: Reconcile contract terms, conditions, recording, and disbursements; an arithmetically balanced statement can still allocate a charge without proper authorization. After opening, escrow gathers instructions, deposits, lender requirements, and title information. The parties complete investigations and required disclosures; the lender underwrites and prepares loan documents. Escrow obtains payoff demands and information needed to clear specified liens and allocate charges. Signing is not always closing. Loan funding, recording, satisfaction of conditions, and disbursement may occur at different points in the sequence. The documents and local process determine the exact order. Possession follows the agreement and may occur later than title transfer. The closing statement records charges and credits. A debit is an amount charged to a party; a credit reduces the amount that party must supply or increases proceeds as appropriate. Not every charge appears as an equal credit to the opposing party: a recording fee paid to a public office is different from a tax proration between buyer and seller.

460.title: Reconcile a simple closing statement
460.text: Assume an $800,000 sale, a $24,000 buyer deposit already in escrow, and $600,000 of new loan proceeds. Before closing costs and prorations, the buyer must provide an additional $176,000. On the seller's side, assume a $300,000 loan payoff and $40,000 of seller charges. The seller's simplified proceeds are $460,000. Both calculations use the same price but account for different obligations. A deposit credit on the buyer's statement acknowledges money already supplied; it is not a seller concession. A loan credit reflects lender funds available toward the price; it is not a reduction of the borrower's debt. A seller loan payoff reduces cash disbursed to the seller; it is not necessarily a tax deduction from the seller's gain. Now add a $900 proration owed by the seller to the buyer. Debit the seller and credit the buyer, reducing seller proceeds to $459,100 and buyer additional funds to $175,100, assuming nothing else changes. A $200 recording fee paid by the buyer instead increases the buyer's requirement without becoming a $200 credit to the seller. This distinction separates transfers between the principals from payments to third parties. Before treating a statement as final, reconcile it with the contract, amendments, payoff demands, and actual funds. An internally balanced statement can still allocate a charge to the wrong party. Arithmetic verification and authorization verification are both necessary.

461.title: Worked scenario: a paid loan still appears
461.text: A seller's statement that a loan was paid requires verification and appropriate title handling, while changed wire instructions require independent authentication. Seller Peyton's preliminary report lists an old deed of trust. Peyton says the loan was paid years ago. The assertion should prompt verification, not automatic deletion. The title provider may need evidence of satisfaction and an appropriate release or reconveyance to insure without that exception. Meanwhile, the buyer receives an email claiming that escrow's bank instructions have changed. The buyer should independently verify with a known, trusted contact method before sending funds. A convincing message or an apparently familiar address is not proof of authorized instructions. The agent's duty of care includes addressing foreseeable transaction risks without treating email as self-authenticating.

462.title: Exam review
462.text: Keep ownership, insurance, and escrow authority separate; a report, a policy, and deposited funds each answer different transaction questions. A preliminary report proposes coverage; the policy provides coverage on its terms. A lender's policy is not the buyer's policy. Escrow follows lawful instructions and holds conditional deliveries; it does not decide disputed ownership of a deposit on one party's demand. Signing, funding, recording, disbursement, and possession are related events that need not occur simultaneously.

463.title: Title insurance and escrow: core distinctions
463.text: Report A preliminary report offers insurance on stated terms, not an abstract's assurance. Coverage The owner and lender insure different interests and may accept different risks. Closing Funds and documents remain conditional until authorized requirements are met.

464.title: A missing easement appears before closing
464.text: A buyer plans deliveries to a small commercial parcel. A preliminary report omitted an access document, but a newly obtained recorded easement limits use in a way that may affect the plan. The buyer's loan is approved and escrow holds a signed deed. No party has yet agreed to accept the newly identified limitation. Discovering a title issue creates three workstreams: determine the actual property right, establish proposed insurance coverage, and resolve contractual closing conditions. Completing one workstream does not silently complete the other two.

465.title: The preliminary report's silence proves clear title.
465.text: Investigate the actual interest and offered coverage. An offer to insure is not a guarantee that no omitted right exists.

466.title: The lender's acceptance binds the buyer's preferences.
466.text: Compare the two insured interests and transaction needs. Protecting collateral is not the same as assuring operational suitability.

467.title: Escrow can fix a disagreement by closing.
467.text: Obtain consistent authorized instructions. Conditional custody is not authority to decide disputed rights.

468.title: A missing easement appears before closing: Classify the new evidence
468.text: Obtain the actual recorded instrument and compare its rights and restrictions with the proposed use and purchase terms. The easement document, property description, and intended delivery pattern matter more than the earlier report's silence. Identify which parcel benefits and what use is actually permitted. A preliminary report is an offer to insure on terms under Insurance Code section 12340.11, not an abstract guaranteeing title's condition. Its omission does not make the easement nonexistent or automatically establish coverage.

469.title: A missing easement appears before closing: Separate coverage from suitability
469.text: Ask the title provider for current requirements and proposed policy treatment, while helping the buyer obtain appropriate advice about access. An updated exception, an available endorsement, or another underwriting response describes insurance treatment. A qualified review addresses whether the legal right supports commercial deliveries. Loan approval or willingness to issue a policy does not prove the buyer's plan works. A lender's collateral concern and the buyer's operational need can lead to different acceptable-risk decisions.

470.title: A missing easement appears before closing: Resolve the contractual decision
470.text: Review applicable title and investigation provisions, deadlines, and available proposals with the buyer before issuing instructions. The purchase agreement and amendments establish the promised condition and response process. The buyer may seek clarification, a permissible cure, or another authorized contractual outcome. Do not promise automatic cancellation or force acceptance of the restriction merely to preserve the scheduled closing. A salesperson communicates and advises within competence; the principal makes the authorized transaction decision.

471.title: A missing easement appears before closing: Align escrow instructions
471.text: Close only after applicable conditions and required approvals are satisfied or properly amended, then reconcile recording and disbursement. The final instructions, lender and insurer requirements, and current title documents must match the authorized bargain rather than the superseded assumptions. A signed deed and deposited funds remain conditional. A unilateral assurance that the buyer will probably accept the problem is not a substitute for authority or required conditions. Before sending funds, independently verify changed wire instructions through an established trusted contact, not a new number supplied in the suspicious message.

472.title: Two insured interests in one transaction
472.text: Two insured interests in one transaction Both policies can exist for the same property because they protect different interests. Neither should be treated as a universal physical-condition warranty. Owner's policy Insures the owner's stated interest. Scope depends on the policy, exceptions, exclusions, and endorsements. Lender's policy Insures the lender's secured interest. Does not serve as the buyer's owner's policy.

473.title: Escrow possession is conditional, not permission to release
473.text: Escrow possession is conditional, not permission to release Funds and a deed can both be present while a required lien release is missing. One party's request does not ordinarily authorize ignoring the other party's closing condition. Conditional escrow A neutral holder safeguards deliveries until authorized closing conditions are met. Buyer funds conditional custody A deposit does not become unrestricted seller money simply because it arrived. Seller deed conditional custody Possession of the signed document does not itself satisfy every closing requirement. Authorized instructions release conditions Required conditions and properly approved changes govern delivery and disbursement.

474.title: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
474.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
474.text: Keep property tax, income tax, transfer tax, and closing allocations separate.

475.title: Four different questions
475.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
475.text: Separate closing cash, income-tax gain, withholding, and property-tax assessment before calculating; similar dollar figures belong to different legal systems. A sale can raise income tax on gain, recurring property tax and reassessment, documentary transfer tax, and tax withholding. These are different systems. A seller can owe transfer tax even when no taxable income gain is recognized. Withholding can be required even when the final tax will be lower, and a federal gain exclusion does not automatically preserve a California property-tax assessment. For examination problems, use the stated assumptions and identify which system is being tested before calculating. For a real transaction, tax advice belongs with a qualified tax professional because filing status, history, entity ownership, depreciation, and exceptions can change the result.

476.title: Basis and gain
476.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
476.text: Determine amount realized and adjusted basis from the appropriate records; current debt, assessed value, and market value are not interchangeable substitutes. Basis is the starting tax investment in the property, commonly cost for a purchase. Adjusted basis incorporates appropriate increases and decreases. Capital improvements can increase basis; depreciation allowed or allowable can decrease it. Ordinary repair costs are not automatically capital improvements merely because the owner paid them before selling. The basic gain relationship is: Amount realized minus adjusted basis equals realized gain. For a simple cash sale, amount realized is generally sale price less qualifying selling expenses. The mortgage payoff affects the cash the seller takes home, but it is not an additional deduction from gain just because escrow pays it. Confusing proceeds with gain is a common mathematical error. An owner buys for $400,000, makes $50,000 of qualifying capital improvements, and sells for $650,000 with $30,000 of qualifying selling expenses. With no other adjustments, basis is $450,000 and amount realized is $620,000. Realized gain is $170,000. A $200,000 mortgage payoff changes cash proceeds, not that gain calculation. Recognized gain is the amount currently taken into taxable income after applicable exclusions or deferrals. Gift and inherited property can follow different basis rules; inherited property generally receives a basis tied to date-of-death value or another applicable valuation rule, while gifts commonly involve carryover-basis rules with special loss limitations. Do not assume every transfer resets basis to market value.

477.title: Follow the dollars through two different calculations
477.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
477.text: Suppose an investment property sells for $900,000 with $45,000 of qualifying selling expenses. The seller's adjusted basis is $520,000 and the loan payoff is $350,000. Amount realized is $855,000, producing $335,000 of realized gain before considering a deferral or other applicable rule. Simplified cash proceeds are $505,000 before withholding and other closing adjustments. The loan balance appears in the cash calculation because proceeds are used to repay the lender. It is absent from the gain calculation because borrowing against the property did not ordinarily create new basis. Refinancing for personal spending can therefore reduce closing cash without reducing taxable gain. A heavily leveraged seller may owe tax even when relatively little cash remains after debt repayment. Basis also requires records. Qualifying acquisition costs and improvements may increase it, while allowed or allowable depreciation can reduce it. The current loan balance, market value, and assessed value are not substitutes. For a gift, the donor's basis and value at the gift can matter; for inherited property, death-date or other applicable valuation rules can matter. The fact that the deed changes names does not tell you the correct basis rule.

478.title: The principal-residence exclusion
478.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
478.text: Apply ownership, use, and prior-exclusion conditions to qualifying gain, not gross price; a replacement purchase is not generally required for the main-home exclusion. Federal law may exclude up to $250,000 of qualifying main-home gain, or up to $500,000 for qualifying married taxpayers filing jointly. The usual framework includes ownership and use for two of the preceding five years and limits involving a prior exclusion. The joint-return rules include their own ownership, use, and look-back requirements. The exclusion concerns gain, not sale price. It is not restricted to taxpayers over a particular age, and qualifying taxpayers need not buy a replacement home to obtain it. Partial exclusions and special rules may apply; depreciation and nonqualified use can limit what is excluded. A personal-residence loss is generally not deductible. In the $170,000-gain example, a qualifying single owner could potentially exclude the entire gain. That does not mean the sale is exempt from every closing tax or filing requirement. Determine each separately.

479.title: Test ownership and use separately
479.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
479.text: A taxpayer can satisfy the ownership test without satisfying the use test. Owning a vacation property for ten years does not by itself establish two years of qualifying main-home use. Conversely, living in a property as a tenant and later purchasing it can create different ownership and occupancy histories. The applicable tests examine both histories rather than asking only when the taxpayer first moved in. For the full $500,000 exclusion on a qualifying joint return, generally either spouse must meet the ownership test, both must meet the use test, and neither may be disqualified by a prior exclusion within the look-back period. The tests need not be satisfied by identical facts for each spouse. Other conditions and special rules still apply, including certain periods of nonqualified use and depreciation. Assume a qualifying single taxpayer realizes $310,000 of gain on the main home and qualifies for the full $250,000 exclusion, with no other adjustments or special rules. The remaining $60,000 is not excluded by that provision. This does not tell you the final tax without applicable rates and the taxpayer's full circumstances. Keep the excluded amount, recognized amount, and resulting tax as separate quantities.

480.title: Like-kind exchange deferral
480.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
480.text: Test exchange eligibility and timing, then distinguish cash boot, recognized gain, and deferred gain; replacement basis preserves rather than erases deferred tax consequences. Section 1031 can defer qualifying gain on exchanges of real property held for investment or productive use in a trade or business. A personal residence and property held primarily for sale do not qualify merely because they are real estate. The exchange must satisfy its legal requirements rather than operate as an unrestricted sale followed by a later purchase. In a typical deferred exchange, replacement property must be identified within 45 days, and receipt generally must occur within 180 days or the applicable tax-return deadline, including extensions, if earlier. Receiving cash or other non-like-kind value, often called boot, can trigger recognition of gain. Deferral is not forgiveness. Basis rules generally carry deferred gain into the replacement investment. A qualified intermediary and other professionals help structure a compliant exchange; a broker should not promise tax deferral after the seller has already received unrestricted proceeds. For a simplified qualifying exchange with only cash boot and no debt or other adjustments, recognized gain is generally limited to the lesser of realized gain or cash received. A $180,000 realized gain and $30,000 cash boot can leave $30,000 recognized and $150,000 deferred. Receiving boot does not necessarily make the entire gain immediately taxable. The deferred amount is preserved through the replacement property's basis rather than forgiven. If replacement property is worth $670,000 and $150,000 of gain is deferred, its simplified basis is $520,000. Different debt, expense, related-party, and property facts can change the calculation. Separate recognition from tax rates, withholding, and the cash available to spend.

481.title: Withholding is a prepayment
481.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
481.text: Federal FIRPTA and California withholding have separate rules; withholding normally prepays tax and can differ substantially from the final liability. Federal FIRPTA rules generally require the buyer to withhold 15% of a foreign seller's amount realized, subject to exceptions and reductions. Qualifying buyer-residence transactions can have no withholding at $300,000 or less and a 10% rate above $300,000 through $1 million. Residence-use requirements and documentation matter. The seller's citizenship label alone does not resolve tax residency. California has separate real estate withholding rules, commonly using 3 1/3% of the sale price or an authorized alternative calculation, unless an exemption applies. Form 593 and current FTB instructions address the transaction. State withholding is not limited to sellers who are foreign persons under FIRPTA. Neither withholding figure is necessarily the seller's final income-tax bill. Treating withholding as an extra commission or a fixed tax on net profit misstates its function. The party responsible for withholding must follow the applicable documentation and remittance rules.

482.title: Apply the appropriate withholding system
482.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
482.text: Consider a foreign seller transferring a property for $800,000 to an individual buyer who satisfies the IRS residence-use requirements. Under the stated FIRPTA residence category, the 10% rate produces $80,000 of withholding, absent another applicable exemption or certificate. If the same purchase is solely for investment and no exception applies, the general 15% rate would produce $120,000. The buyer's intended and qualifying use changes the analysis. California withholding must still be evaluated independently. A federal exemption does not automatically establish a Form 593 exemption. Likewise, a California principal-residence exemption determination does not replace verification of federal foreign-person status. The same seller may require different documentation under the two systems. Withholding can reduce the seller's closing cash but normally functions as a tax prepayment credited through the applicable filing process. The amount may exceed or fall short of final liability. A salesperson should identify the issue early enough for escrow and qualified tax advisers to obtain required certifications and instructions rather than discovering the cash impact only after the seller has committed the proceeds elsewhere.

483.title: Property tax after transfer
483.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
483.text: Distinguish due dates from delinquency dates and reassessment from existing bills; closing prorations do not necessarily settle later supplemental assessments. California's regular property-tax fiscal year runs July 1 through June 30. Secured-tax installments are due November 1 and February 1 and ordinarily become delinquent after December 10 and April 10, subject to calendar adjustments. Due and delinquent are different dates. A qualifying ownership change can trigger reassessment and supplemental assessment. The seller's existing tax bill therefore may not predict the buyer's future property-tax bill. Closing prorations often use available information, while a supplemental bill arrives separately. Do not assume that an impound account or closing statement has already covered every future assessment. Proposition 19 permits qualifying replacement-residence base-year-value transfers for specified homeowners, including those at least age 55 and eligible disabled or disaster-affected owners, subject to requirements. Its intergenerational exclusion is narrower than the former broad parent-child rules: qualifying family homes or farms, continued qualifying use, value limits, and timely claims matter. A child inheriting a rental house does not automatically inherit its low assessed value. Indexed limits should be checked with BOE rather than memorized as permanently fixed.

484.title: Transfer tax and prorations
484.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
484.text: Use the stated tax base and day-count convention, then assign debits and credits according to who already paid or collected the item. The common county documentary transfer tax authorized by Revenue and Taxation Code section 11911 is $0.55 per $500, or fraction, of the applicable taxable value. Value of qualifying liens remaining on the property is excluded under that provision. City taxes and local rules can add costs. A new purchase loan is not automatically a remaining old lien for this calculation. If the stated taxable amount is $620,000 and only that county rate applies, divide by $500 to obtain 1,240 units, then multiply by $0.55: $682. Round units upward when a fractional $500 unit exists, not to the nearest whole unit. For prorations, identify who already paid or collected the item and who should bear it for each period. Suppose annual taxes are $7,200 and the problem specifies a 360-day year. The daily amount is $20. If the seller owes 40 days that remain unpaid and the buyer will pay them, debit the seller and credit the buyer $800. If the seller already prepaid the buyer's 40-day share, reverse those entries. Use actual-day or 30-day conventions only when the problem or instructions specify them.

485.title: Rent and taxes run in opposite directions
485.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
485.text: A seller receives the full $3,000 rent for a thirty-day month before a sale. The contract assigns the first ten days to the seller and the remaining twenty days to the buyer. The seller collected $2,000 belonging economically to the buyer's period, so debit the seller and credit the buyer $2,000. That entry reallocates income already received. Now assume the seller prepaid $600 of a charge covering the same month and the contract uses the same allocation. The buyer owes twenty-thirtieths, or $400, so debit the buyer and credit the seller $400. The direction reverses because the seller advanced an expense for the buyer's period. Netting the two prorations produces a $1,600 credit to the buyer, but calculate each separately before combining them. Do not invent who owns the closing day. A question may assign that day to either party or specify an exact count. Nor should an annual charge automatically use a 360-day year unless the stated convention permits it. First identify the amount, covered period, allocation, and payment status. The debit and credit then follow from who owes whom.

486.title: Exam review
486.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
486.text: Label each calculation before using a percentage or subtraction; correct arithmetic on debt, basis, proceeds, or taxable gain cannot repair a mistaken category. Cash proceeds are not taxable gain. Exclusion is not deferral, and withholding is not final liability. A property-tax reassessment exclusion is not an income-tax exclusion. On arithmetic questions, write the calculation base and day-count convention before multiplying; correct arithmetic on the wrong base still produces the wrong answer.

487.title: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations: core distinctions
487.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
487.text: Three gains Realized, recognized, and deferred gain are different quantities. Cash Debt payoff and withholding affect cash without necessarily reducing realized gain. Carryover Deferral usually preserves gain through replacement basis rather than forgiving it.

488.title: Cash boot without losing the entire deferral
488.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
488.text: Assume a fully qualifying investment-property exchange. Relinquished property has a $700,000 fair market value and $400,000 adjusted basis. The taxpayer receives replacement real property worth $650,000 plus $50,000 cash. There is no debt, exchange expense, depreciation-recapture complication, related-party issue, or other adjustment. The exercise isolates ordinary cash boot; eligibility and timing are stipulated, not inferred from these numbers. Recognized gain is a current tax category, deferred gain is preserved for later treatment, and basis carries that preservation forward. These figures do not prove exchange eligibility; actual transactions require timely identification, receipt, and compliance with the other governing requirements.

489.title: Any boot makes the whole exchange taxable.
489.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
489.text: Compare realized gain with the relevant boot under the applicable rules. Cash can cause partial recognition rather than destroy every deferral.

490.title: Deferred means permanently excluded.
490.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
490.text: Track the replacement property's basis. A lower basis preserves gain for later tax treatment.

491.title: The replacement property's price is always its tax basis.
491.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
491.text: Apply the relevant exchange-basis rules. A qualifying exchange differs from an ordinary fully taxable purchase.

492.title: Cash boot without losing the entire deferral: Find realized gain
492.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
492.text: Relinquished property value $700,000 Adjusted basis $400,000 Replacement property value $650,000 Cash received $50,000 700000 - 400000 300000 The exchange produces $300,000 of economic gain before applying the nonrecognition rule. Receiving real property rather than only cash does not prevent gain from being realized. The $650,000 replacement value plus $50,000 cash accounts for the $700,000 received in this simplified exchange.

493.title: Cash boot without losing the entire deferral: Limit current recognition
493.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
493.text: Relinquished property value $700,000 Adjusted basis $400,000 Replacement property value $650,000 Cash received $50,000 min(300000, 50000) 50000 With only the stated cash boot and no complicating adjustments, recognize the lesser of realized gain and cash received. The taxpayer does not recognize the whole $300,000 merely because some cash was received. Conversely, boot cannot create recognized gain greater than the total gain actually realized.

494.title: Cash boot without losing the entire deferral: Identify deferred gain
494.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
494.text: Relinquished property value $700,000 Adjusted basis $400,000 Replacement property value $650,000 Cash received $50,000 300000 - 50000 250000 The remaining $250,000 is deferred, not permanently excluded. This number is not a tax payment, a lender payoff, or additional spendable cash. The final tax on the recognized portion depends on applicable tax rules and the taxpayer's circumstances, none of which are supplied by this calculation.

495.title: Cash boot without losing the entire deferral: Carry the deferral into basis
495.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
495.text: Relinquished property value $700,000 Adjusted basis $400,000 Replacement property value $650,000 Cash received $50,000 650000 - 250000 400000 Subtract deferred gain from the replacement property's fair market value to obtain its simplified $400,000 basis. A later taxable sale can therefore reveal the preserved gain. Assigning a fresh $650,000 basis while also deferring $250,000 would improperly erase the very gain the exchange rules postponed.

496.title: Cash boot without losing the entire deferral: Test an unchanged-value later sale
496.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
496.text: Relinquished property value $700,000 Adjusted basis $400,000 Replacement property value $650,000 Cash received $50,000 650000 - 400000 250000 If the replacement property were later sold in a fully taxable sale for the same $650,000 value, with no intervening basis changes or selling expenses, the gain would be $250,000. That matches the amount previously deferred. Do not subtract the earlier $50,000 recognized gain again; it was already accounted for in establishing replacement basis.

497.title: Sale proceeds are not the same as taxable gain
497.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
497.text: Sale proceeds are not the same as taxable gain With an assumed $500,000 adjusted basis, realized gain is $760,000 amount realized minus $500,000 basis = $260,000 before any exclusion or deferral. The loan payoff affects cash, not that gain calculation. Illustrative selling price 800000 Assumed selling expenses -40000 Loan payoff -300000 Illustrative cash proceeds 460000 Before other settlement debits, credits, or withholding.

498.title: Payment status determines the proration direction
498.lessonTitle: Transfer taxes, gain, withholding, and prorations
498.text: Payment status determines the proration direction Use the stated day count and closing-day allocation. Income already collected and expenses already advanced can produce opposite entries for the same ownership period. Who has already paid or received the amount allocated to the other party? Seller prepaid buyer expense The seller advanced a charge allocated to the buyer's period. Debit buyer; credit seller. Buyer will pay seller expense The seller's allocated share is unpaid and will be paid by the buyer. Debit seller; credit buyer. Seller collected buyer rent The seller already received rent allocated to the buyer's period. Debit seller; credit buyer.

499.title: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
499.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
499.text: Recognize transfers that depend on death, court authority, or operation of law.

500.title: Authority replaces the ordinary owner signature
500.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
500.text: Determine the event, authorized signer, and required approvals before accepting a special-purpose deed; a title alone does not establish valid sale authority. In an ordinary sale, the living owner or an authorized representative executes the transaction. Special transfers require a different source of authority: death and succession law, a trust, a court order, a foreclosure power, or another statute. The salesperson's first task is to identify who has authority to act and what conditions limit that authority. A relative who has keys is not necessarily entitled to list a decedent's house. A beneficiary who expects to inherit is not necessarily the current title holder or authorized estate representative. A lender that holds a deed of trust has security rights, but not unlimited permission to sell outside the applicable foreclosure process. Distinguish ownership claims from power to administer. The person entitled to receive value from an estate may not be the person authorized to sign the deed during administration. Title and escrow providers commonly require evidence of capacity, appointment, powers, and any relevant orders.

501.title: Death does not produce one universal process
501.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
501.text: A will names beneficiaries and may nominate an executor, but appointment and the property's existing ownership determine who can act. A person who dies with a valid will is testate; a person whose property is not disposed of by a valid will may be intestate as to that property. A will directs disposition but does not itself guarantee that probate can be avoided. A person can also die partly testate and partly intestate if the will does not dispose of all probate property. Probate administration addresses assets, debts, claims, taxes, and distribution under court authority. An executor is nominated in the will and serves after the required appointment. An administrator is appointed when an executor does not serve, commonly where there is no will. Both are personal representatives and owe duties to the estate and interested persons. Intestate succession determines heirs under statute. It is not a rule that the closest person who volunteered to maintain the house owns it. Marital property characterization and family relationships can affect shares. If no entitled private successor exists under the governing law, escheat may result in property passing to the state.

502.title: A will, an appointment, and a deed do different work
502.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
502.text: Suppose a will leaves a house to a niece and nominates a nephew as executor. The niece is the intended beneficiary of that disposition; the nephew is the proposed administrator of the estate in the executor role. Neither fact alone shows that either person may immediately sign a listing or deed without the required authority. Court appointment and the scope of powers must be established where probate administration is necessary. The estate may need to pay debts or expenses before distributing property. A specific gift in a will does not guarantee the beneficiary will receive the asset unaffected by valid claims and administration requirements. Conversely, the personal representative's control during administration does not make the house the representative's personal property. For a transaction file, useful evidence can include the death certificate, relevant title documents, court letters, orders, and other authority documents appropriate to the proceeding. The exact requirements belong to the governing law and title review. A salesperson should identify the correct capacity and obtain verification, not choose a signer based on family seniority, possession of keys, or who first called the office.

503.title: Nonprobate transfers
503.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
503.text: Trust ownership, survivorship, life estates, and qualifying summary procedures can avoid ordinary probate steps, but their actual requirements still matter. Some property passes outside ordinary probate. Valid joint-tenancy survivorship can transfer the deceased joint tenant's interest to surviving joint tenants. Community property with right of survivorship can provide a similar specified transfer mechanism. Appropriate documents are still needed to establish the death and update the record; survivorship does not mean the public title record updates itself. A properly funded trust allows the trustee to administer property under the trust's terms. A successor trustee's sale is not automatically the same as a court-confirmed probate sale. Review trust authority and any limits. A person named as a beneficiary is not necessarily empowered to sign for the trust. A valid transfer-on-death deed can transfer qualifying property under its statutory requirements. It is not equivalent to simply writing a beneficiary's name on an ordinary deed and leaving it unrecorded in a drawer. Execution, witnessing, recording, revocation, and beneficiary rules require compliance with the current statute. California also provides simplified procedures for qualifying estates and property. For deaths on or after April 1, 2025, the primary-residence petition procedure under Probate Code sections 13151-13154 uses a $750,000 limit, subject to its other conditions. This is a simplified court process, not an exemption for every estate asset. Other procedures have different limits, and periodic adjustments are scheduled. Eligibility depends on property type, value, date of death, and the particular procedure; an old single "small estate limit" does not control every transfer.

504.title: Compare death, sale, and termination of a life estate
504.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
504.text: A life tenant's death ends that life estate according to its terms. The succeeding interest may belong to a remainderman or revert to the grantor or successors, depending on how it was created. The life tenant's will does not ordinarily convey a life estate beyond the measuring life. This differs from a fee owner's death, which leaves an inheritable ownership interest to be administered or transferred. Trust property presents another distinction. The successor trustee may have authority to sell under the trust even though no personal representative has been appointed for that property. But the trust must actually hold the relevant interest; merely signing a trust document without transferring the house into it does not establish that the house is administered as trust property. Survivorship requires verification as well. A deed originally creating joint tenancy may have been affected by a later conveyance or severance. The correct answer follows the interest existing at death, not an assumption based on how the owners first purchased. These examples explain why a death certificate answers who died but does not, by itself, identify every successor or signing authority.

505.title: Selling through probate
505.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
505.text: Check the representative's powers and applicable notice or confirmation process; independent administration does not remove fiduciary obligations or every procedural condition. A personal representative may sell estate property under the authority granted by the court and applicable law. Some sales require court confirmation; others may proceed under the Independent Administration of Estates Act with full authority and required notices, subject to objections and restrictions. Limited authority does not confer every power available under full authority. In a confirmation sale, the accepted offer can be subject to a hearing and qualifying overbids. The initial buyer should understand that acceptance by the representative is not necessarily the final transfer. The process protects the estate's interests, and the court evaluates statutory requirements rather than merely honoring whichever buyer arrived first. For an ordinary private real property sale requiring confirmation under Probate Code section 10309, both the appraisal and its valuation date must be within one year before the confirmation hearing, and the offered sum must be at least 90% of that appraised value. Statutory exceptions exist. Probate commissions are governed by the applicable contract and court authority; a salesperson should not assume the same payment procedure as an unrestricted private sale. Under Probate Code section 10311, the statutory minimum first overbid generally adds 10% of the first $10,000 of the accepted bid and 5% of the amount above $10,000. The hearing can involve further bidding and procedural requirements. This formula does not determine every later increment or apply to every trust or independently administered sale.

506.title: Independent administration is still administration
506.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
506.text: The Independent Administration of Estates Act can permit a personal representative with the required authority to act without obtaining a separate confirmation order for every qualifying sale. That does not eliminate fiduciary duties, notice requirements, restrictions in the appointment, or the effect of a proper objection. Full authority and limited authority must not be treated as identical. A buyer considering an estate sale should determine whether court confirmation is required and whether the offer is subject to additional procedural conditions. A transaction advertised as "probate" might proceed differently from another probate transaction because the representative's authority differs. The label alone does not establish an overbid hearing or guarantee that no hearing will occur. The representative must also distinguish estate expenses from personal expenses and handle proceeds for the estate. A brokerage should not disburse sale funds to a beneficiary merely because everyone expects that person eventually to inherit. Distribution authority, creditor claims, taxes, and the governing order or administration process may require a different destination and timing.

507.title: Worked overbid
507.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
507.text: Calculate the ordinary first-overbid minimum from the accepted bid, then separately examine appraisal requirements, bidder responsibility, terms, and judicial discretion. Suppose an accepted bid of $500,000 is presented for court confirmation and the statutory first-overbid formula applies. Ten percent of the first $10,000 is $1,000. Five percent of the remaining $490,000 is $24,500. Add both increments to $500,000 to obtain $525,500. Do not add 10% to the entire $500,000. Do not subtract the first $10,000 from the final bid. The first segment and the remaining segment use different rates, and both increments are added to the accepted bid. Deposit, qualification, and hearing rules must also be met; the arithmetic alone does not qualify someone to bid.

508.title: Appraisal threshold and overbid are separate calculations
508.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
508.text: Assume a private estate sale requires confirmation, the qualifying appraisal is $600,000, and no exception to the ordinary 90% rule applies. The threshold is $540,000. An accepted $550,000 offer clears that threshold. The first-overbid formula then uses the accepted $550,000 offer as its base, not the $600,000 appraisal. Ten percent of the first $10,000 is $1,000. Five percent of the remaining $540,000 is $27,000. Add $28,000 to the accepted offer to obtain $578,000. The $540,000 figure has two different appearances here: it is the minimum appraisal-based price and coincidentally the portion of the accepted bid above $10,000. Those are different calculations, and different numbers would eliminate the coincidence. If the accepted bid were only $520,000, computing an overbid would not by itself cure the original confirmation problem under the stated assumptions. First determine whether the sale satisfies applicable requirements. Then calculate the bidding threshold if the procedure calls for one. Price, bidder responsibility, payment terms, and judicial discretion remain separate considerations. Meeting the numerical first-overbid minimum is not an unconditional entitlement to confirmation. Probate Code section 10311 also addresses a responsible bidder, legal compliance, the court's discretion to order a new sale, and differing cash or credit terms. The formula uses the bid without deducting a broker's commission. A mathematically sufficient offer can still fail a different requirement.

509.title: Other involuntary and court-related transfers
509.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
509.text: Foreclosure, deed in lieu, partition, condemnation, and bankruptcy transfer interests through different processes; none universally removes every prior property right. Foreclosure enforces a security interest through the applicable judicial or nonjudicial process. A trustee's sale under a deed of trust and a judicial foreclosure are different procedures. Lien priority determines which interests may be extinguished and which may survive; buying at foreclosure does not guarantee a property free of every lien. A deed in lieu of foreclosure is a voluntary conveyance to the lender as an alternative to completing foreclosure. Because it is not the foreclosure process itself, junior interests are not automatically eliminated. The lender examines title and the parties' settlement carefully. A tax sale follows statutory enforcement of tax-defaulted property. A sheriff's sale can arise from execution of a judgment. A partition proceeding resolves cotenant interests through division or, when appropriate, sale and allocation of proceeds. Condemnation is the legal proceeding through which government exercises eminent domain, ordinarily requiring just compensation under the governing standards. Bankruptcy can place property under federal court control and impose an automatic stay. A creditor or broker should not assume that ordinary enforcement or closing can continue unchanged after learning of a filing. Court authority, trustee powers, liens, and exemptions may determine the next steps.

510.title: A special deed does not answer every title question
510.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
510.text: An investor buys at a foreclosure sale and later learns that a senior deed of trust remains. The phrase "foreclosure property" did not promise a debt-free asset. Determine the lien foreclosed, its priority, the procedure, and which interests survived. A deed in lieu raises a different issue because a voluntary conveyance does not perform the same extinguishment process. Partition and condemnation also differ in purpose. Partition resolves competing ownership interests among cotenants through division or sale as appropriate. Condemnation implements a public acquisition under eminent-domain authority. Both can involve a court and a resulting conveyance, but neither should be classified as ordinary probate merely because a judge participates. The exam method is to identify the event, the authority, and the resulting interest. Death, default, unpaid taxes, cotenant disagreement, and public acquisition trigger different rules. The name of the resulting deed helps identify the process, but the proceeding and valid authority determine what the buyer receives.

511.title: Transfers through operation of law
511.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
511.text: Ownership can change through legally recognized events without an ordinary negotiated deed, but each asserted process still requires its own elements. Adverse possession can produce ownership after strict requirements are satisfied, including California's generally applicable five-year period, qualifying possession, and payment of assessed property taxes. It is different from a prescriptive easement, which concerns a use right rather than title. Public property is subject to protective rules that defeat ordinary adverse-possession assumptions. Accession can alter ownership boundaries through events such as gradual accretion, subject to the governing water and boundary law. Dedication can create public rights through the owner's acts and required acceptance. These are not ordinary broker-negotiated conveyances, but they can affect what interest a seller actually has.

512.title: Exam review
512.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
512.text: Trace authority, procedure, and the interest transferred independently; a high price or familiar deed label does not cure missing approval. Identify the authority, proceeding, and interest transferred. A will does not itself avoid probate; a trust sale does not automatically require court confirmation; an expected heir cannot automatically sign for an estate. Apply the probate overbid formula only when the question makes it relevant, and never assume a special-purpose deed erases all prior rights.

513.title: Probate, court sales, and other transfers: core distinctions
513.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
513.text: Authority Identify the representative's actual authority, not just family or beneficiary status. Procedure Probate confirmation, independent administration, and nonprobate transfers differ. Bidding The appraisal floor and first-overbid increment use different bases.

514.title: The appraisal floor is not the overbid
514.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
514.text: An ordinary probate private sale requires court confirmation. The appraisal and valuation dates satisfy the applicable one-year requirements, and the appraised value is $840,000. The accepted bid is $780,000. Apply the ordinary ninety-percent appraisal threshold and the statutory first-overbid calculation. Assume no exception changes these numerical rules; all other confirmation requirements remain separate. Use the appraisal only for the appraisal requirement and the accepted bid only for the overbid increment. Then return to authority and procedure. The arithmetic is a threshold analysis, not a substitute for examining whether the court may confirm this particular offer.

515.title: Ninety percent of appraisal is the overbid.
515.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
515.text: Calculate the two requirements independently. They use different bases and serve different purposes.

516.title: Subtract commission before calculating the increment.
516.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
516.text: Use the accepted bid as the statute directs. Compensation does not redefine the statutory bid amount.

517.title: The highest numerical offer must always win.
517.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
517.text: Check responsibility, terms, legal compliance, and discretion. A sufficient number does not satisfy every confirmation condition.

518.title: The appraisal floor is not the overbid: Check the appraisal floor
518.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
518.text: Appraised value $840,000 Accepted bid $780,000 Appraisal threshold 90% of appraised value First-overbid increment 10% of first $10,000; 5% of remainder 840000 * 0.90 756000 The accepted $780,000 bid exceeds the $756,000 floor. This comparison addresses the ordinary private-sale appraisal requirement, not the amount a competing bidder must offer. A bid below this floor is not cured merely by correctly calculating an increment from an inadequate accepted price.

519.title: The appraisal floor is not the overbid: Calculate the first bracket
519.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
519.text: Appraised value $840,000 Accepted bid $780,000 Appraisal threshold 90% of appraised value First-overbid increment 10% of first $10,000; 5% of remainder 10000 * 0.10 1000 The first $10,000 of the accepted bid receives a ten-percent increment, producing $1,000. Do not apply ten percent to the full $780,000 or to the appraisal. The statute uses a two-part increment because the first bracket and the remaining bid have different rates.

520.title: The appraisal floor is not the overbid: Calculate the remaining bracket
520.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
520.text: Appraised value $840,000 Accepted bid $780,000 Appraisal threshold 90% of appraised value First-overbid increment 10% of first $10,000; 5% of remainder 770000 * 0.05 38500 Subtract the first $10,000 from the accepted bid, leaving $770,000. Five percent of that remainder is $38,500. The commission is not deducted to create a net accepted bid for this formula. A broker's compensation question is separate from the statutory calculation base.

521.title: The appraisal floor is not the overbid: Add the increment to the bid
521.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
521.text: Appraised value $840,000 Accepted bid $780,000 Appraisal threshold 90% of appraised value First-overbid increment 10% of first $10,000; 5% of remainder 780000 + 1000 + 38500 819500 The calculated minimum first overbid is $819,500. Reaching that amount does not establish an unconditional right to purchase. Responsible-bidder requirements, legal compliance, cash or credit terms, and the court's statutory discretion can still affect confirmation or result in a new sale.

522.title: The appraisal floor is not the overbid: Verify with an equivalent expression
522.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
522.text: Appraised value $840,000 Accepted bid $780,000 Appraisal threshold 90% of appraised value First-overbid increment 10% of first $10,000; 5% of remainder 780000 * 1.05 + 500 819500 For an original bid of at least $10,000, five percent of the entire bid plus an extra $500 produces the same increment as the two statutory brackets. The extra $500 supplies the additional five percent on the first $10,000. This arithmetic cross-check does not remove appraisal, bidder, terms, or court-approval requirements.

523.title: After a death, identify title and authority first
523.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
523.text: After a death, identify title and authority first This is a classification map, not a finding that a particular estate qualifies for a procedure. Heirship, a will, and legal authority to sign a sale instrument are different questions. How was this interest held? Survivorship interest Determine whether a valid survivorship form controls. Verify the documents needed to establish the survivor's title. Trust-held interest Determine the successor trustee and powers granted. Verify trustee authority and transaction requirements. Estate interest Determine whether probate or another authorized procedure applies. Verify representative authority and any court requirements.

524.title: Build the first overbid from the accepted offer
524.lessonTitle: Probate, court sales, and other transfers
524.text: Build the first overbid from the accepted offer Assume this court-confirmed sale uses the stated statutory formula. The accepted offer, not the appraisal, supplies this base; bidder eligibility and court requirements remain separate. Accepted offer subject to the stated first-overbid rule 550000 10% of the first $10,000 1000 5% of the remaining $540,000 27000 Calculated first-overbid minimum 578000 $550,000 accepted offer + $28,000 combined increments.

525.title: Licensing, supervision, and consumer protection
525.text: Who may perform licensed work, how brokers supervise it, and how California enforces professional standards.

526.title: The activity determines the license
526.text: Identify the act, expected compensation, person represented, and actual exemption before deciding whether the worker needs an active license and broker affiliation. A real estate license gives permission to perform defined activities; it is not a general credential for every business connected with land. California ordinarily requires a broker license when a person, for compensation or in expectation of compensation, acts for another to sell, buy, lease, negotiate, solicit, or perform other statutorily defined real estate services. Arranging certain secured loans and selling business opportunities also fall within the law. One transaction can be enough. Calling a fee a consulting payment does not change the underlying activity. An owner dealing with the owner's own property generally is not acting for another. Other exemptions exist for specified persons and functions, including certain court-appointed fiduciaries. Exemptions have boundaries: being an attorney, accountant, relative, or experienced investor does not create unrestricted authority to conduct a brokerage business. On the exam, identify who owns the property, whose interests the worker serves, what the worker actually does, and whether compensation is expected. A salesperson performs licensed activity through an employing or responsible broker. Passing the examination alone is insufficient. The license must be issued and effective, and the necessary broker affiliation must exist before the salesperson begins licensed work. A salesperson cannot independently establish a brokerage merely by creating a company or calling the business a real estate team.

527.title: Supervision is an operating responsibility
527.text: Reasonable supervision requires implemented procedures, document review, and responses to warning signs; a contractor agreement or delegated task does not erase responsibility. The responsible broker must maintain reasonable supervision over transactions and personnel. This includes reviewing documents, establishing trust fund procedures, monitoring advertising, maintaining records, preventing discrimination, and making sure personnel understand their authority. An office manual that nobody implements is not effective supervision. Nor does an independent-contractor agreement eliminate the broker's duties under licensing law. A broker can assign operational tasks to qualified people, including a branch manager where applicable. Delegation does not automatically eliminate the responsible broker's accountability. A salesperson should elevate unusual contract language, trust shortages, disputed releases, suspected fraud, and demands to conceal defects. These are matters for timely professional judgment, not problems to hide until closing. The salesperson normally receives compensation for licensed work through the responsible broker. A seller cannot bypass that relationship by paying the salesperson a separate negotiating fee directly. Referral compensation also requires attention to licensing and the service performed. A broker cannot pay an unlicensed person for performing acts that required a license simply because the payment occurs after closing.

528.title: Assistants can support, but cannot replace, licensees
528.text: An assistant may transmit approved information or schedule events, but independent negotiation, substantive advice, and selection of transaction terms cross the clerical boundary. The distinction between administrative work and licensed work is functional. An assistant may organize files, schedule inspections, obtain status information, deliver approved materials, and perform permitted document preparation under supervision. An assistant may check whether signatures are present; the licensee makes the final determination about compliance and advises the client about consequences. An assistant cannot independently explain which counteroffer to accept, negotiate price, solicit a particular listing through substantive persuasion, or interpret an agreement for a buyer. At an open house, handing out prepared brochures and arranging contact with the licensee differ from conducting a property showing or answering negotiating questions. A broker's presence does not transform prohibited conduct into authorized conduct. Consider a caller asking when an inspection report will arrive. The assistant can obtain its delivery status. If the caller asks whether the report justifies canceling the purchase, the assistant should transfer the question to a licensee. This boundary remains the same whether communication occurs by telephone, text, social media, or a website chatbot. Technology does not acquire a license by automating the conversation.

529.title: Initial qualification and renewal
529.text: Passing an examination, meeting renewal education requirements, and holding present authority to practice are separate milestones; a late-renewal opportunity does not authorize intervening work. Salesperson applicants ordinarily must be at least 18 and complete the required prelicense education, including Real Estate Principles, Real Estate Practice, and an approved additional course, before satisfying examination and licensing requirements. Required practice-course content includes fair housing and implicit bias. Honesty and disclosure in the application process matter independently of a passing score; fingerprints and background review are part of licensing. California real estate licenses generally run for four years. Renewal ordinarily requires 45 hours of DRE-approved continuing education completed within the applicable period. For a salesperson's first renewal, current requirements include specified courses in ethics, agency, trust funds, risk management, fair housing with an interactive component, and implicit bias, plus minimum consumer-protection coursework. Broker requirements and later renewals have different mandatory-course arrangements. A salesperson should not apply the broker's first-renewal list without checking the correct category. Late renewal may be available within two years after expiration, but that opportunity does not authorize licensed activity during the lapse. Limited exemptions and extensions have their own requirements. The practical lesson is to distinguish eligibility to renew from present authority to practice, and initial education from continuing education.

530.title: Records make conduct reviewable
530.text: Retain the transaction's evidence, not merely its final contract; electronic messages and instructions can explain representations, receipt, authority, and delivery. Business and Professions Code section 10148 generally requires brokers to retain transaction records for three years from closing or, if a transaction is not consummated, from the listing date. The statutory categories include listings, receipts, canceled checks, trust records, and other documents obtained or executed in connection with transactions requiring a license. Special laws or circumstances may justify or require longer retention. Electronic records must remain accessible, accurate, and reproducible for examination. Keeping only the final contract can omit important offers, instructions, disclosures, and evidence of delivery. Deleting a message because the application labels it a chat does not eliminate its significance to a transaction. A defensible file tells the story of what was represented, authorized, received, and delivered.

531.title: Discipline and financial recovery serve different purposes
531.text: Administrative discipline addresses licensing conduct, while civil remedies and the limited Recovery Account have different purposes, eligibility rules, procedures, and financial limits. DRE licenses and regulates real estate professionals and can investigate, impose appropriate administrative sanctions, suspend or revoke licenses, and issue orders concerning unlicensed activity. Grounds can include fraud, substantial misrepresentation, trust fund violations, and failure of supervision. An ordinary commission disagreement does not automatically establish a disciplinary violation, and a DRE complaint is not a substitute for a civil damages action. The Consumer Recovery Account, historically called the recovery fund, provides limited compensation for eligible actual, direct losses involving licensee fraud or trust fund conversion in transactions requiring a license. The claimant must satisfy statutory procedures, ordinarily including a qualifying final judgment, award, or order and collection requirements. The current maximum is $50,000 per transaction and an aggregate $250,000 per licensee. Multiple victims do not each receive an unlimited separate transaction cap.An application generally must be filed within one year after the qualifying determination becomes final.Payment can trigger license suspension until statutory repayment requirements are met.

532.title: Worked scenario
532.text: A license lapse and an assistant's unauthorized showing create separate authorization problems; the broker must reassign work rather than rely on pending renewal. Morgan's license expired yesterday. A renewal application is being prepared, and the broker asks Morgan to negotiate a buyer's counteroffer while an unlicensed assistant handles the open house alone. Neither instruction solves the authorization problem. Morgan must stop licensed work during the lapse; the assistant must remain within permitted administrative duties. The broker should reassign negotiations and licensed showing work to properly authorized personnel, document the arrangements, and correct the office's expiration tracking. If a later dispute arises, complete records let the broker distinguish a communication error from unauthorized activity. A client's loss would not automatically qualify for the Consumer Recovery Account: the claimant must show the specific statutory basis and satisfy the recovery process.

533.title: Apply the licensing test to a workflow
533.text: Changing from typing a licensee's chosen terms to independently choosing a contingency changes the activity, even when the same standard form is used. Consider three workers at the same property. The owner's employee schedules a repair, a brokerage assistant sends an approved inspection appointment, and a salesperson recommends a counteroffer. Although all work concerns real estate, the legal analysis is not identical. Identify the act, whether it is performed for another, whether compensation is expected, and whether a specific exemption applies. Then determine whether the individual is properly authorized within the required broker relationship. Do not start with a job title and work backward toward an exemption. An assistant may type information supplied by the licensee into an approved form without independently selecting the terms. If the assistant chooses the contingency period based on the buyer's needs, the task has changed from clerical preparation to substantive judgment. Likewise, transmitting an already authorized message differs from bargaining over whether the seller should pay for repairs. A script or supervisor's eventual review does not necessarily make an otherwise licensed act clerical. Suppose a team leader tells an assistant to call potential sellers and persuade them that now is the right time to list. Calling the worker a marketing coordinator does not change the solicitation. A safer workflow separates permitted contact or scheduling functions from the licensed conversation and provides an immediate transfer to an authorized person. The relevant DRE guidance is function-specific; an office should train workers on boundaries, not simply hand them a list of approved job titles.

534.title: Build supervision around evidence
534.text: Design supervision around actual risks and evidence; repeated late deposit documentation calls for investigation before a financial loss is established. A responsible broker cannot personally attend every conversation, but can implement controls that make problems visible. Before assigning a transaction, verify authorization and relevant experience. During the transaction, review material documents, changes, advertising, deadlines, and money handling. After closing or cancellation, check that the retained file includes the instructions and disclosures needed to explain what occurred. These controls should match the brokerage's activities: a firm holding rent reserves has different operational exposure from one sending every purchase deposit directly to neutral escrow. For example, a salesperson repeatedly turns in deposit receipts several days late. The absence of a known loss does not make the pattern harmless. The broker should investigate when the funds actually arrived, where they went, whether required deadlines were met, and whether the office's instructions were followed. Coaching alone may be insufficient if access or assignment changes are needed. A signed acknowledgment of the office manual is evidence of training, not proof that later transactions complied. The same reasoning applies to a remote branch. Digital access to files can support supervision, but only if someone reviews the relevant information and follows up. A manager's appointment is not permission for the responsible broker to ignore warning signs. The appropriate exam answer usually addresses the conduct and the oversight process rather than treating delegation as a complete transfer of responsibility.

535.title: Separate the remedy from the complaint
535.text: Match the requested result to the available process, and never confuse correcting records or renewing a license with retroactively authorizing earlier conduct. Imagine a buyer alleges that an agent deliberately concealed a serious defect and seeks repayment of repair costs. Several processes may arise from the same facts. DRE examines licensing violations. A court or other authorized forum determines civil claims and available relief. An association may evaluate its member's code obligations. Each has different authority, procedures, and potential outcomes; filing in one place does not automatically accomplish the purpose of another. The Consumer Recovery Account is narrower than general errors-and-omissions coverage. An unsuccessful investment, a normal commission disagreement, or simple dissatisfaction with service does not by itself satisfy its eligibility rules. Even an eligible fraud loss must pass through the required determination and collection process. If several people claim losses from the same transaction, the transaction limit matters collectively, and the licensee aggregate remains a separate ceiling. The existence of two ceilings does not allow a claimant to choose whichever yields more. Finally, distinguish correcting a problem from erasing it. Renewing an expired license restores authority only as applicable prospectively; it does not make earlier unauthorized negotiations proper. Reconstructing missing records may help explain a file, but fabricated or backdated records create a new problem. An exam scenario that offers concealment as an efficient solution is testing honesty and accountability as much as the underlying licensing rule.

536.title: Exam review
536.text: Resolve licensing questions by function, authority, supervision, and remedy; avoid answers that treat job labels, client consent, or subsequent renewal as universal permission. Identify the licensed act before analyzing a worker's title or payment method.A salesperson acts through the responsible broker; supervision cannot be waived by contract.Clerical delivery and status reporting differ from negotiation and advice.A renewal opportunity is not permission to practice with an expired license.DRE discipline, civil remedies, and Consumer Recovery Account payments are separate processes.

537.title: Licensing, supervision, and consumer protection: core distinctions
537.text: Activity first Licensing follows what a person does for another, not the worker's title. Delegation is limited A manager can perform assigned work without eliminating the responsible broker's supervision. Remedies differ DRE discipline, civil damages, and Consumer Recovery Account eligibility require separate analyses.

538.title: A counteroffer arrives during a license lapse
538.text: A remote team receives a counteroffer while its lead salesperson's license is expired. An unlicensed coordinator knows the file, the branch manager is available, and the client wants an immediate response.
